title.en: Every French noun has a gender

shortRule.en: Every noun is masculine (le) or feminine (la) — the article is part of the word.

explanation.en: French sorts all nouns into two grammatical classes, masculine and feminine. This is a property of the word itself, not of the thing it names, so the reliable way to learn a noun is to learn it together with its article: 'le chat', 'la pomme'. The good news: a noun's ENDING often signals its gender, and the upcoming lessons teach only the ending patterns that a 36,940-noun analysis shows to be genuinely dependable.

note.en: before a vowel sound the article shortens to l', hiding the gender — eau is feminine

exceptions.en: Before a vowel sound, both le and la become l', so the article stops showing the gender. For those nouns, remember them with un/une instead: une eau minérale.

shortRule.en: Nouns ending in -tion, -ance, -ence, -ité or -ie are almost always feminine.

explanation.en: You do not have to memorize every noun's gender one by one — the ending often decides it. In an analysis of 36,940 French nouns, words ending in -tion are feminine 99.5% of the time, -ance 98.9%, -ence 98.3%, -ité 97.8%, and -ie 96.3%. When you meet a new noun with one of these endings, say « la » with confidence.

exceptions.en: "Almost always" is not "always": le silence (-ence) and le génie (-ie) are everyday exceptions — but with reliability this high, guessing feminine is the right habit.

shortRule.en: Nouns ending in -ment, -age, -eau or -ier are usually masculine.

explanation.en: The masculine side has strong ending patterns too, from the same 36,940-noun analysis: -ment is masculine 99.8% of the time, -age 98.5%, -eau 96.7%, and -ier 97.1%. Meet a new noun with one of these endings and « le » is very likely right.

exceptions.en: l'eau (water) and la peau (skin) are feminine — the famous exceptions to -eau.
l'image (the picture), la page, la plage (the beach) and la cage are feminine -age words: -age is "usually", not "always".

shortRule.en: -on is usually masculine — but the -tion/-sion family is feminine, and so are la maison, la raison, la saison. -eur is usually masculine — with famous feminine exceptions.

explanation.en: Two common endings hide sub-patterns. Nouns in -on are masculine 96.7% of the time ONCE you set aside the -ion and -son words — and those two groups are mixed, not simply feminine. The dependable feminine sub-families are -tion/-sion (la question, la télévision — 99% feminine) and -aison/-ison (la maison, la raison, la saison, la prison). Outside them, -ion and -son words are often masculine: l'avion, le camion, le lion, le poisson, le poison, le blouson. And -eur nouns are masculine 92.5% of the time, but several very frequent ones are feminine. Learn the sub-families, not just the last two letters.

exceptions.en: Frequent feminine -eur nouns: la peur (fear), l'erreur (the mistake), la couleur (the color), la fleur (the flower).

The -aison/-ison sub-family: la maison, la raison, la saison, la prison, la comparaison — feminine (la chanson and la boisson too). But le poisson, le poison, le son and le saucisson are masculine — check the article.

memoryHint.en: See -tion, -sion, -aison or -ison? Think la. Other -on — le patron, le poisson, le garçon — think le.

title.en: Être and avoir — the two anchor verbs

shortRule.en: je suis / tu es / il est · j'ai / tu as / il a — learn these six forms cold.

explanation.en: The two most-used verbs in French are also the most irregular, so their présent forms are learned as words, not from a pattern: être (to be) — je suis, tu es, il/elle est, nous sommes, vous êtes, ils/elles sont; avoir (to have) — j'ai, tu as, il/elle a, nous avons, vous avez, ils/elles ont. They repay the effort twice: they carry everyday sentences now, and later they build the past tense for every other verb.

translations.en: You are right (literally: you have reason).

exceptions.en: French uses avoir where English uses be in fixed phrases: avoir faim (to be hungry), avoir raison (to be right), avoir 20 ans (to be 20 years old).
Before a vowel, je shortens: j'ai, never 'je ai'.

memoryHint.en: sont = they are, ont = they have — the s belongs to être.

shortRule.en: parle, parles and parlent are all pronounced the same — endings change on paper more than in speech.

explanation.en: Regular -er verbs (the largest verb family) all conjugate like parler: je parle, tu parles, il/elle parle, nous parlons, vous parlez, ils/elles parlent. In speech those six forms collapse to three sounds — parle/parles/parlent all sound like 'parl' (Lexique 4 phonology: /paʁl/), parlons has its own sound, and parlez sounds exactly like the infinitive parler (/paʁle/). So when you speak, the pronoun does most of the work; the written endings matter most when you type or write.

note.en: vous: stem + ez — sounds like the infinitive

exceptions.en: Verbs in -ger keep the e before -ons to protect the soft g: nous mangeons, never 'mangons'.
Aller looks like an -er verb but is irregular: je vais, tu vas, il va.

memoryHint.en: If the subject is je/tu/il/ils, an -er verb usually SOUNDS like its bare stem.

title.en: Talking about the future with aller

shortRule.en: aller (présent) + infinitive = going to: Je vais manger — I am going to eat.

explanation.en: French has a simple future you can use from day one: conjugate aller in the présent and follow it with any infinitive, exactly like English 'going to'. Je vais parler (I'm going to speak), tu vas manger, nous allons habiter à Lyon. You only ever conjugate aller — the second verb stays in the dictionary form — so six memorized forms of aller unlock future statements with every verb you know.

examples.target: Nous allons parler avec le patron.

translations.en: We are going to talk with the boss.
They are going to take a trip.

exceptions.en: Aller alone also means physically going somewhere: Je vais au bureau — I am going to the office. Context tells you which reading is meant.

memoryHint.en: aller + infinitive works just like English 'going to + verb'.

shortRule.en: avoir (présent) + past participle = did / have done: J'ai mangé — I ate.

explanation.en: The everyday French past tense is built from two pieces you already have: the présent of avoir plus the verb's past participle. For -er verbs the participle just swaps -er for -é (parler → parlé, manger → mangé), so J'ai parlé = I spoke, Tu as mangé = you ate, Nous avons habité = we lived. Some verbs have participles to memorize — être → été, avoir → eu, faire → fait — but the frame never changes.

exceptions.en: A small set of movement/change verbs (aller among them) build this tense with être instead of avoir: Je suis allé — I went. That set is taught as its own list later.

memoryHint.en: -er verb? Its participle is the infinitive sound spelled -é.

shortRule.en: A French noun in -tion is almost always the same word as in English — and feminine.

explanation.en: You already know a large stock of French: of the 16 -tion nouns frequent enough for this course's corpus-derived candidate pool, 15 are the same word in English — solution, question, direction, situation, attention, information, condition, conversation… (opération just swaps é for e). The gender comes free too: across the 36,940-noun analysis, -tion nouns run 99.5% feminine (1,895 measured), so say la solution, la direction — and remember l' hides the la in l'attention.

note.en: feminine — the l' just hides it

exceptions.en: félicitation is the pool's one non-transparent -tion word: Félicitations ! means Congratulations!
The words are shared, the sounds are not — French -tion says /sjɔ̃/, never /shun/.

memoryHint.en: See -tion? Trust the meaning, say la.

shortRule.en: -té usually turns into English -ty: la liberté → liberty.

explanation.en: The -té ending is a bridge to English -ty: 10 of the 16 -té nouns in the everyday pool map straight across — liberté→liberty, réalité→reality, société→society, sécurité→security, université→university, identité→identity… Six of them are real vocabulary to learn, not cognates — for example santé (health), vérité (truth), volonté (will) and été (summer). Gender: 91.6% of the 1,031 -té nouns are feminine; the masculine exceptions include le côté (the side), l'été and un invité (a guest). Bonus family for later: French has 616 nouns in -isme mirroring English -ism, 99.8% masculine — none crack the everyday top-1500.

note.en: NOT "santy" — a real word to learn

exceptions.en: Non-cognates in the family: santé = health, vérité = truth, volonté = will, été = summer.
Masculine exceptions to feminine -té: le côté, l'été, un invité.

memoryHint.en: -té → -ty, and la — unless it is le côté or l'été.

shortRule.en: Some French words look English but mean something else — learn each trap together with its repair word.

explanation.en: A few high-value French words are traps: they look like English words they do not mean. La librairie is the bookshop — the library is la bibliothèque. La journée is the day(time) — a journey is un voyage. La monnaie is your change in coins — money in general is l'argent. Rester means to stay, never to rest, and attendre means to wait, never to attend. The fix is to learn each trap as a pair: the French word with its real meaning, plus the French word for what it fooled you into thinking.

exceptions.en: More traps for later: sensible means sensitive, actuellement means currently, assister à means to attend.

memoryHint.en: La librairie sells books; la bibliothèque lends them.

shortRule.en: Singles to 16, dix-compounds to 19, then tens + hyphen — except 21, 31… which take "et un".

explanation.en: French numbers are a system, not a list. 0–16 are single words (zéro … seize). 17–19 compound with dix: dix-sept, dix-huit, dix-neuf. The tens vingt, trente, quarante, cinquante, soixante attach their unit with a hyphen — vingt-deux, cinquante-huit — except at one, where French says vingt et un, trente et un … soixante et un. Two spellings are official: the traditional 'vingt et un' and the 1990 rectified 'vingt-et-un'. This course shows the traditional forms and accepts both when you type.

exceptions.en: The "et" appears only at 21, 31, 41, 51, 61 — and at 71.

memoryHint.en: Hyphens everywhere; "et" only before un (and onze at 71).

shortRule.en: 70 is soixante-dix (sixty-ten); the seventies keep counting through the teens.

explanation.en: France French has no separate word for seventy. 70 is soixante-dix — sixty-ten — and the decade rides the teens: 72 soixante-douze (60+12), 75 soixante-quinze, 77 soixante-dix-sept, 79 soixante-dix-neuf. 71 is the one 'et onze': soixante et onze. If you hear soixante, wait for the rest of the number before writing anything down.

exceptions.en: Belgium and Switzerland say septante (septante-cinq = 75). Recognize it — this course teaches and grades France French.

shortRule.en: 80 is quatre-vingts (4 × 20); the -s drops only when another number follows (quatre-vingt-un), and the 80s/90s never take "et".

explanation.en: 80 is quatre-vingts — literally four twenties — and it keeps its plural -s unless another number follows: quatre-vingts, quatre-vingts euros, but quatre-vingt-un, quatre-vingt-deux… (and no 'et' before un here). The nineties stack the teens on top: 90 quatre-vingt-dix, 91 quatre-vingt-onze, 99 quatre-vingt-dix-neuf. And 100 is simply cent.

note.en: nothing follows — keeps the -s (quatre-vingts euros too)

exceptions.en: Belgium and Switzerland say nonante for the nineties (nonante-deux = 92). Recognition only — France French is graded here.

memoryHint.en: quatre-vingts loses its -s the moment another number follows.

shortRule.en: le, la, je, ne, de, que, ce drop their vowel before a vowel sound: l'eau, j'ai, n'est pas, c'est.

explanation.en: French refuses to let two vowel sounds collide across these little words. Before a word starting with a vowel sound, le and la become l' (l'eau, l'homme), je becomes j' (j'ai), ne becomes n' (ce n'est pas), de becomes d', que becomes qu', and ce becomes c' (c'est). This is not optional or casual — writing 'je ai' is simply wrong. The apostrophe is the visible trace of the dropped vowel, and it is why dictionary entries like eau hide their gender behind l'.

exceptions.en: Elision needs a vowel SOUND, not just a vowel letter — and some h-words refuse it entirely (see the two h's).

memoryHint.en: Two vowel sounds may never touch: drop the first, write an apostrophe.

shortRule.en: A silent final consonant can wake up before a vowel: les amis sounds like "layz-ah-mee".

explanation.en: In connected speech, some silent final consonants attach to a following vowel. After the little words — determiners and pronouns — the link is required: les amis (the s wakes up as a z sound and starts 'amis'), nous avons, vous êtes, un petit enfant (t links). But liaison is forbidden after et (et ici — no link), after a singular noun (le chat est — the t of chat stays silent), and before certain h-words. Between those poles there is a polite-register middle ground you will meet later; for now, trust the required links after les/des/nous/vous/ils/elles.

note.en: s links as a z sound

exceptions.en: No liaison after et, after a singular noun, or before an h aspiré word (les héros — no link).

memoryHint.en: Little word + vowel = link it. After et: never.

shortRule.en: Every French h is silent — but h muet words elide and link (l'histoire), h aspiré words refuse both (le héros).

explanation.en: No French h is ever pronounced, yet h-words split into two families. H muet behaves like a vowel: l'histoire, l'homme, l'hôtel — elision applies, and liaison links (les hommes: z sound). H aspiré behaves like a consonant even though you hear nothing: le héros (never l'héros), and les héros has no link at all. You cannot hear the difference in the h itself — only the words around it reveal which family a word belongs to, so learn h-words together with their article.

exceptions.en: Dictionaries mark h aspiré with a star or apostrophe before the entry. When in doubt, the le/l' test tells you the family.

memoryHint.en: Hero keeps his distance: LE héros. Stories let you in: L'histoire.
